title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Does economic development cause political development — and if it does, in which direction does the causal arrow run?


Ishiyama surveys three answers that disagree about almost everything: where to look, what the unit of analysis is, and whether the Western path can be repeated at all.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 3.
Frame it against Chapter 2. There, the explanation was historical sequence. Here, the explanation is economic structure — and the three schools fight over whether that structure is internal, international, or something the state itself can choose.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

State what modernization theory claims and name the main versions of “political development” inside it
Distinguish social mobilization from political institutionalization, and explain why Huntington needs both
Explain how dependency theory inverts the modernization story
Say what statism adds that neither of the other two can explain
Compare all three on the dimensions in Table 3.4

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: Modernization theory

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Older than political science
Modernization theory is “less a coherent theory than an approach.” Its roots run back to the Enlightenment conviction that people can change their own conditions.







Condorcet
Technology and economic transformation let humankind alter its moral and cultural values


Saint-Simon (1760–1825)
Economic development and technology can better social conditions


Comte (1798–1857)
Modernization ushers in a “positive” scientific era


Marx
Industrialization of the economic base changes the social and political superstructure





The common thread: economic change comes first, and political change follows.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Durkheim: complexity and anomie
Durkheim asked what industrialization does to the division of labour.

All societies must perform certain functions — security, political leadership, spiritual leadership
What differs is the complexity of the division of labour that performs them
Simple societies need little complexity to hold order; industrial capitalism forces functional differentiation



Anomie. Older certainties — God above all — are called into question by science and technology, producing a widespread sense of rootlessness, and with it criminality and social violence.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3; Durkheim ([1893] 1964).
Connect back: this is the same disruption Chapter 2 called the storm. Durkheim gives it a psychological mechanism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Parsons: traditional and modern as ideal types
text:
Parsons: traditional and modern as ideal types
Table 3.1 · Traditional vs. modern societies









Traditional societies
Modern societies




How is social status determined?
Ascriptive status
Achievement status


What social roles do people play?
Diffuse roles
Specific roles


Are values universal or case-dependent?
Particularistic values
Universalistic values


Which matters more, group or individual?
Collectivity orientation
Self-orientation


Immediate reward, or postponed for future benefit?
Affectivity
Affective neutrality





These are ideal types anchoring a continuum, not descriptions. No society is purely one or the other — every real society sits somewhere between.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Table 3.1, after Parsons (1951, 1971).
Ishiyama is careful here and students often are not: ascription has not vanished from modern societies — he names race, ethnicity and gender explicitly — and achievement is not absent from poor ones.
Affectivity vs affective neutrality is the row worth explaining: in traditional societies people act to meet immediate needs; in modern ones, basic needs being met, people forgo present satisfaction for future gain. Mill called it enlightened rationality.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lipset: the strong claim
In Political Man (1959) Lipset argued for a direct relationship between industrialization and political democracy.

Economic modernization creates the social requisites of democracy: a large, vibrant, literate middle class, and wealth
He found direct correlations between democracy and higher urbanization, higher literacy, and greater per capita income



From correlation he concluded causation: economic development has a direct causal relationship with political democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Deutsch: not democracy — mobilization
Karl Deutsch (1961) accepted the disruption but refused Lipset’s conclusion.

the process in which the major cluster of old social, economic and psychological commitments are eroded or broken and people become available for new patterns of socialization and behavior
— Deutsch (1961, p. 494), defining social mobilization


Industrialization moved populations from countryside to city. People who had identified with a locality now made new acquaintances, learned new things, and questioned their own identity — which is how national identities emerged.



Politically, mobilization expands “the politically relevant strata of the population” — those persons who must be taken into account. Whether that ends in stability or disorder depends on how the existing system copes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Almond and Coleman: five crises
Economic modernization creates crises a political system must resolve. What results depends on how it copes.







Crisis
What it is




Identity
Local ties break; a new sense of community — usually national — must form


Legitimacy
Divine right gives way to the idea that rule rests on the consent of the governed


Participation
A “revolution in rising expectations” generates demands to take part in governing


Penetration
New institutions must link rulers to ruled directly, replacing indirect rule through nobles


Distribution
New social groups demand their material share of the economic pie




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, citing Almond and Coleman (1960; text gives 1966), The Politics of the Developing Areas.
The penetration crisis is the one students find least intuitive. Before modernization, kings ruled through local nobles who collected the taxes and kept considerable autonomy — including warring with each other. Direct rule had to be built.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What is “political development”?
The term does not mean one thing, and the disagreement matters.


Lipset
A politically developed state is one that is democratic.

Beer (1973)
Development is the expansion of the bureaucratic state — patterns of interests create patterns of power, which generate new interests, ad infinitum.

Huntington (1965, 1968)
Development is political institutionalization: “the process by which organizations and procedures acquire value and stability.”



Notice what follows. On Beer’s and Huntington’s definitions, a country can develop politically without becoming any more democratic.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Huntington’s four dimensions
How do you tell whether a political system is institutionalized?







Dimension
The question




Adaptability / rigidity
Can it survive a change in its environment?


Complexity / simplicity
Is there a division of labour, with redundant structures?


Autonomy / subordination
Is it independent of any single social group?


Coherence / disunity
Is there a unity of purpose holding it together?




Adaptability has three measures: chronological age, generational age (how many leadership transitions), and functional age (how many times it has changed what it does).

Ishiyama’s example for functional age is worth telling. The YMCA began as a religious body for young Christian men, took on recreation, then women, then everyone — and survives as something quite different. The Women’s Christian Temperance Union achieved national prohibition in 1919, could not adapt to another function, and disappeared.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: what does institutionalization measure?
Huntington’s generational age measures a system’s adaptability by counting:

The number of years since the organization was founded
The number of leadership transitions it has been through
The number of times it has changed its function
The number of social groups it represents



The second. A system can be chronologically ancient and still fragile if one leader has never been replaced.


[Key] The second. The first is chronological age and the third is functional age — both are real Huntington measures, which makes them good distractors; the student has to keep three similar terms apart.
Ask for a contemporary example of an old system with a low generational age. It is a fast route into the succession problem, which their China/Vietnam and Hungary/Poland teams will meet directly.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two variables, four outcomes
Table 3.2 · Huntington’s classification of regime types




Institutionalization high
Institutionalization low




Social mobilization high
Civic
Corrupt (praetorian)


Social mobilization low
Contained
Primitive




Table 3.3 · Country examples









Institutionalization high
Institutionalization low




Social mobilization high
The United States · Great Britain · the Soviet Union
Most of the developing world


Social mobilization low
Contained — perhaps colonial societies
Traditional agrarian monarchies (Imperial Ethiopia)






Outcomes are the product of the interaction of the two, not of either alone. Mobilization without institutions is not development but decay.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The entry that should stop you
text:
The entry that should stop you

The Soviet Union is filed under civic — beside the United States and Great Britain.


Ishiyama’s reasoning: the USSR modernized massively and fast in the 1930s, generating extensive mobilization pressure. The system was complex, autonomous, and armed with a legitimising ideology, so it met those demands — or contained them by repression and violence — and survived.



Britain and the United States built institutions before industrialization, which Chapter 2 treated as something close to a historical accident. The Soviet Union built the state and transformed the economy at the same time — rather like building a ship in a stormy sea.


This is the payoff slide for the whole first half. It also shows the cost of Huntington’s definition: if development is institutionalization rather than democracy, a totalitarian state can be a developmental success.
Worth naming aloud: Huntington, at least in the 1960s work, appeared to favour a one-party solution for the developing world. Ishiyama lays out the argument — one-party states are more complex than personalist dictatorships, allow interests to be articulated internally, are autonomous, and rely on rules rather than individuals — and notes India’s Congress, Japan’s LDP, and Mexico’s PRI as long dominant-party cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Modernization theory in summary
Whatever version, three commitments recur:

Political development is a consequence of economic development — the political system evolves in response to economic stimuli
The approaches rest on historical observation of the West, particularly Europe
The key intervening variable is often political culture — the subject of Chapter 4



Point 2 is the opening dependency theory will attack, and it is the same parochialism Macridis complained about in Chapter 1.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Dependency

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: A different room, a different answer
text:
A different room, a different answer
While modernization theory developed among North American political scientists, a rival grew in post-war Latin America, rooted in neo-Marxism and dissatisfied with the international economic order.







Prebisch (1950)
Research at ECLA: falling wealth in poor countries correlates with rising wealth in rich ones


Baran (1957) · Frank (1966, 1967)
International capitalism produced the de-development of the developing world


dos Santos (1970)
A “new dependency” — external relations are articulated internally


Cardoso
Growing disparities between centre and periphery, written in exile


Wallerstein (2004)
The “World System” and the history of international capitalism




Cardoso is worth a sentence: he wrote as a dependency theorist in exile and later served as President of Brazil — and governed as something closer to an orthodox reformer. Students enjoy the irony, and it opens the question of whether the theory implies any workable policy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The development of underdevelopment
Frank’s claim, introduced to an American audience in 1966: poverty in the developing world is not a starting condition that development will cure. It is a product of world capitalism.


The Indian textile case. Before the British East India Company, textile production — largely household industry — employed a great many people and was extensive. Cheap manufactured imports followed the British, destroyed the indigenous industry, and created mass unemployment and poverty.



So the periphery is not “behind.” It was actively de-developed.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Two more breaks with modernization theory
text:
Two more breaks with modernization theory
1 · The international system is missing. Modernization theory explains development by internal structural factors, with no reference to the international environment.

2 · The Western path is assumed repeatable. Marx himself wrote, in the 1867 preface to Das Kapital, that “the country that is more developed industrially only shows, to the less developed, the image of its own future.”



Dependency’s reply: the West industrialized before the world capitalist system consolidated — indeed the West created it. Countries developing now face an obstacle their predecessors never had to pass.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.1 · Imperialism, nineteenth century






Figure 1: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.1. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.1 and surrounding text.
Note for the instructor: the source file we worked from carries the chapter’s text and tables but not its artwork, so this diagram is a faithful reconstruction from the caption and the paragraphs around it, not a scan of the original.
The line to land is the last one. The surplus does not merely enrich the core — it is spent on reform at home, which is why the revolution Marx predicted in the industrial core did not arrive.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.2 · Neo-imperialism, twentieth century






Figure 2: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.2. FDI, foreign direct investment. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.2 and surrounding text. Reconstruction, as above.
The maquiladora example does the work: parts are farmed out rather than finished goods produced, so the value added — and the profit — is captured on the other side of the border. Ask what a country could do about that, and you have arrived at statism before the next section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Figure 3.3 · The internal articulation






Figure 3: Recreated from Ishiyama, Figure 3.3. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Figure 3.3; Amin (1974, 1976); Frank (1967). Reconstruction, as above.
This is the figure that explains why dependency theory is a theory of politics and not only of economics. The comprador bourgeoisie is the hinge: a propertied class with no interest in dismantling the order that enriches it, allied with feudal landlords, and hostile to empowering the masses.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Why dependency implies authoritarianism
In the West the bourgeoisie was the progressive class — it dismantled feudalism and opened the way to democracy.

In the periphery the comprador bourgeoisie is nothing of the kind. Its wealth comes from trade, not industrial production, so it has no reason to change the system, and every reason to keep the masses unempowered.



And if a populist leader does emerge from the masses — usually through the ranks of the military — he is likely to reject bourgeois democracy as Western and corrupt. So from this perspective there is little hope for democracy while dependent relations persist.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: what does “de-development” claim?

Poor countries have not yet begun the development process
Poverty in the periphery is a product of the expansion of world capitalism, not a starting condition
Development stalls because peripheral states adopt the wrong values
Peripheral countries will eventually resemble the core, as classical Marxists expected



The second. The periphery is not behind. It was actively made poor.


[Key] The second. The third is modernization theory’s answer, and the fourth is the classical Marxist expectation — Lenin, Luxemburg, Kautsky — which neo-Marxist dependency theory explicitly denies.
That fourth option is worth dwelling on: classical Marxists expected capital to relocate to the periphery as wages rose in the core, eventually producing a peripheral bourgeoisie and proletariat and the conditions for international revolution. Dependency theory says that never happens.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Statism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The anomaly
Classical dependency says the periphery can never catch up. But some countries plainly did.

Japan · Russia · Turkey, and more recently the Asian Tigers — Taiwan, Singapore, South Korea.


Scholars trained in the dependency tradition — Evans, Rueschemeyer, Skocpol — began to question whether dependency travelled beyond Latin America. Some peripheral countries were catching up, and doing it through state-led industrialization.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What both other theories missed
The statist critique: modernization theory and dependency theory are both society-centred. Each ignores the role the state itself plays in capital accumulation and investment.



Liberal state
An arena in which interests compete.

Marxist state
A tool of the dominant class.

Weberian state
“A human community which claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.”




In the first two the state is an object with no interests of its own. For Weber it is a community — so it has interests, and the paramount one is survival.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Politics as the cause
What drives a state to modernize is the threat posed by external enemies. Rapid industrialization raises military capacity, and military capacity buys security.


So the arrow reverses. For modernization theory politics reflects internal economic change; for dependency it reflects external economic structure. For statism, politics is a cause of economic transformation.


Link forward to the team project. Statism is the school that gives a constitutional engineer something to do — it is the one that treats state action as a choice rather than a reflection. That is the same move the course makes in Chapter 1’s neo-institutionalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Comparing the three

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Table 3.4 · The three approaches compared










Modernization theory
Dependency
Statism




Unit of analysis
State
Global system
State


Can earlier models be replicated?
Yes
No
Yes


Economic development is possible…
when modern values are adopted
only when the international economic order changes
as the result of voluntaristic action by the state





Read the middle row as the fault line. If earlier models cannot be replicated, then every reform proposal built on a Western template is answering the wrong question.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 3, Table 3.4.
For modernization theory the models are the developed West; for the statists they are the state-led industrializers — Japan, Turkey. Same answer on the row, different exemplars.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: whose unit of analysis?
Which approach takes the global system rather than the state as its unit of analysis?

Modernization theory
Dependency theory
Statism
All three, since each studies countries in an international context



Dependency. For modernization theory and statism alike the unit is the state — development is a function of what happens inside a country’s borders, or of what its state chooses to do.


[Key] Dependency theory. The fourth option is the plausible-sounding trap: it is true that all three are aware of the international environment, but only dependency theory makes the world system the thing being analysed.
This is the item most worth connecting to their own projects. A team whose diagnosis is entirely domestic has implicitly chosen modernization theory or statism — and should say so rather than stumble into it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s own summing up: there is broad consensus that the economic environment is a crucial explanatory factor for the emergence of political forms, including democracy — while the debate over how it matters remains open.


Chapter 4 turns to the variable modernization theory kept treating as the intervening step: political culture.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
For your dossier
Round 2 asks for a context diagnosis including political economy. This chapter gives you three incompatible ways to write that section.
Three things to try this week:

Ask which of the three approaches your focal country’s trajectory best fits — and which one your comparator fits. If they differ, that difference is your Round 3 argument
Locate your focal country on Huntington’s two dimensions. Is its problem mobilization, institutionalization, or the gap between them?
If your team is drawn to a structural explanation, name the mechanism linking structure to politics. Haggard and Kaufman’s complaint about structural theories was precisely that the mechanism goes missing

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lecture 1: What does comparison explain?

Comparative politics is both a subject and a method.


By the end of today, you should be able to:

distinguish comparative politics from country description;
explain the many variables, few cases problem;
recognize most-similar and most-different designs; and
connect the field’s history to our constitutional-engineering project.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Open with the central question and preview the four learning outcomes.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Start with a comparison


Taiwan

Semi-presidential system
Mixed electoral rules
Competitive democracy


South Korea

Presidential system
Mixed electoral rules
Competitive democracy




What could this pairing help us explain—and what could it not establish by itself?


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Take two quick responses. The aim is to surface the difference between noticing variation and designing a comparison.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s comparative-method framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The book begins with a problem
text:
The book begins with a problem
Ishiyama does not organize the course as a tour of countries.

He organizes it around a practical question:

Under what conditions can political democracy develop—and when will institutional engineering fail?




Theories become useful when applied to a consequential problem.
Institutional choices must fit historical, economic, social, cultural, and international conditions.
Democracy is not assumed to be easy, inevitable, or universally transplantable.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Emphasize problem-based learning and the conditional—not prescriptive—character of the question.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction, opening section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A problem-based course
Problem → diagnose a focal country’s political constraints
Comparison → use a shadow case to test explanations
Design → evaluate institutional alternatives and trade-offs
Defense → explain why the recommendation fits the evidence


The goal is not to discover a perfect constitution. It is to make a defensible comparative claim.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Connect the chapter directly to the semester project.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction, opening and “The Plan of this Book.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Defining comparative politics

Transition: We know the course problem. Now define the field that will help us solve it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three definitions compete

The study of foreign countries
The study of comparative government
A subject and method of political inquiry



Ishiyama adopts the third definition: systematic comparison of political phenomena within political systems.



The United States is therefore one case among many—not a separate universe.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Cold call: Which definition would exclude the United States, and why is that limiting?
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Subject and method work together


As a subject
Political phenomena within a state, society, country, or political system:

institutions;
behavior; and
political ideas.


As a method
Systematic comparison used to:

identify similarities and differences;
discover patterns; and
explain variation.



Suggested time: 2 minutes. Stress that a country report is not automatically comparative politics.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), drawing on Wiarda, Mahler, and Lim.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Comparative politics asks “why?”


Description
How does a legislature work?
Who selects the executive?
What electoral formula is used?

Explanation
Why did this institution emerge?
Why does it produce different outcomes elsewhere?
Under what conditions will it change?



Description supplies evidence. Comparison turns evidence into an explanation.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Ask students to turn one descriptive question into an explanatory question.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Macridis and the traditional approach.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Within states—or between them?







Comparative politics
International relations




Politics primarily within political systems
Politics primarily between political systems


Elections, parties, courts, executives, identity, participation
War, alliances, trade, diplomacy, international organizations


Why outcomes vary across cases
Why states and other actors interact as they do




The boundary is useful, but not absolute: international forces also shape domestic politics.

Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. Use EU politics or foreign election interference as a boundary case.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The comparative method

Transition: The field’s subject is broad. Its distinctive leverage comes from research design.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The central constraint
Imagine explaining the Russian Revolution with one case.

Military defeat and wartime strain?
Economic and social transformation?
Bolshevik organization and Lenin’s leadership?
Paralysis at the top of the imperial regime?



Many plausible causes + one observed outcome = weak causal leverage.



Lijphart’s formulation: comparative politics often has too many variables and too few cases.

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Cold call: Why can evidence consistent with a theory still fail to prove that theory?
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Lijphart (1971).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three strategies for causal leverage








Strategy
How it controls alternatives
Main constraint




Experiment
Randomization and a control group
Countries cannot usually be assigned to treatments


Statistical method
Estimates several relationships at once
Requires enough cases and defensible measures


Comparative method
Selects cases to hold key factors constant
Conclusions depend heavily on case-selection logic





The comparative method is a quasi-experimental strategy for a small number of cases.


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Briefly distinguish experimental control, statistical control, and control by case selection.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of experimental, statistical, and comparative methods.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Most-Similar Systems Design
Compare cases that are similar on relevant background conditions but differ on the outcome or institution of interest.


Similar cases + different outcome → investigate the remaining difference.



This is Mill’s Method of Difference.

Strength: controls many rival explanations through case selection.
Risk: the cases may differ in an unnoticed but consequential way.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Introduce MSSD as a logic, not a claim that cases are identical.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), MSSD discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Estonia and Latvia illustrate MSSD
Both cases shared important conditions before the Soviet collapse:

annexation in 1940;
indigenous and Russophone populations;
relatively high Soviet-era development;
unitary, roughly parliamentary systems.










Key difference
Latvia
Estonia




1989–90 electoral rule
Single-member plurality
Single Transferable Vote





Different party-system development could then be investigated through the electoral-rule difference.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Stress “investigated,” not mechanically “proved.” Ask what omitted difference might still matter.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Estonia–Latvia example; Ishiyama (1993).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Cold call: defend a pairing
Return to Taiwan and South Korea.

What important conditions does the pairing approximately hold constant?
What institutional or political difference could provide leverage?
What unmeasured difference could undermine the comparison?



A defensible comparison identifies both its leverage and its limits.


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Cold-call one student for each question, then invite one amendment from the room.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s MSSD framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Most-Different Systems Design
Compare cases that differ widely but share the same outcome.


Different cases + same outcome → search for a common cause.



This is Mill’s Method of Similarity.

Strength: a shared factor may travel across diverse contexts.
Risk: different causal paths can generate the same outcome.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Introduce equifinality: the same outcome can have multiple causes.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), MDSD discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Design check
Scenario A
Two economically and culturally similar democracies adopt different electoral systems and develop different party systems.
Scenario B
Three societies with different histories, economies, and institutions all experience democratic breakdown after elected leaders disable checks and balances.

Which is MSSD? Which is MDSD? What would each comparison need to measure?

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Ask for the design first, then the dependent variable and candidate explanatory factor.
[Sources] - Instructor examples based on Ishiyama’s comparative-design framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
How the field evolved

Transition: The field’s history is a recurring debate over what counts as knowledge and what political inquiry is for.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two tensions organize the history


Normative ↔︎ empirical
Should scholars ask what political order ought to be—or explain what can be observed?

Understanding ↔︎ application
Is the purpose to build general knowledge—or improve political institutions?



Comparative politics repeatedly moves between these poles rather than permanently choosing one side.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use these tensions as the thread through the historical sequence.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “The Evolution of Comparative Politics.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Plato and Aristotle offer two traditions
text:
Plato and Aristotle offer two traditions


Plato

Knowledge through reason and insight
Emphasis on justice and the ideal order
Foundation of a normative tradition


Aristotle

Approximately 150 constitutions as evidence
Comparison of institutions and social foundations
Foundation of an empirical tradition



Both nevertheless asked how political life might be improved.

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Use the cave briefly, but do not let it displace the comparative point.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Plato and Aristotle.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Aristotle classified regimes



Rule by
Public-serving form
Self-serving form




One
Monarchy
Tyranny


Few
Aristocracy
Oligarchy


Many
Polity
Democracy




For Aristotle, “democracy” meant corrupt rule by the many—not the modern idea of constitutional democracy.


His larger claim: mixed government supported by a strong middle class was more stable than pure oligarchy or pure democracy.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Clarify the historical meaning of “democracy” before students interpret the table using modern definitions.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Aristotle and Table 1.2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Comparison revived with a changing world
text:
Comparison revived with a changing world

Exploration exposed Europeans to political systems beyond Europe.
Modern states developed distinct institutions, economies, and political cultures.
Renaissance science restored confidence in observation and systematic inquiry.




Machiavelli
Compared political practices to find models that rulers could emulate.

Montesquieu
Compared political systems and advanced separation of powers—but also made dubious climate-based claims.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use climate theory as a reminder that comparison can generate bad inference as well as insight.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Middle Ages and Enlightenment discussion.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Marx and Weber disagree about causation
text:
Marx and Weber disagree about causation


Marx
Economic relations and class power shape political and social institutions.
Primary causal emphasis: political economy

Weber
Culture, religion, institutions, and political leadership have partly autonomous effects.
Primary causal emphasis: multicausal explanation


Cold call: What evidence would distinguish these explanations?

Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Ask students to name an observable implication rather than choose a favorite theorist.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), discussion of Marx and Weber.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The American field started descriptively
Early twentieth-century American comparative politics largely emphasized:

European governments;
formal and legal institutions; and
description of legislatures, executives, and courts.


World War II and the Cold War increased demand for knowledge about:

rebuilding Germany and Japan;
Soviet and communist politics;
decolonization and political instability; and
democratic development.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Note how world events and funding priorities shaped the field’s agenda.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), American comparative politics and the behavioral revolution.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Categories can distort what we observe
text:
Categories can distort what we observe
Ishiyama recounts an example from precolonial West Africa:

some communities selected “kings” by rotation among notable families;
British officials interpreted kingship as hereditary;
indirect rule converted a rotating office into a life appointment inherited by heirs.



Using a familiar European label obscured the institution—and colonial policy then changed it.



Comparison requires concepts that travel without erasing local meaning.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Treat this as the chapter’s warning about conceptual stretching and parochialism.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), West African example in the Macridis discussion; Crowder (1968).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The behavioral revolution changed the unit of analysis

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Easton put politics inside an environment
text:
Easton put politics inside an environment
Environment supplies demands and support
↓
Political system converts inputs into authoritative decisions
↓
Outputs reshape society and the international environment
↺ Feedback creates new demands and support

The system includes government, parties, interest groups, and leaders—not only formal institutions.

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Walk once around the input–conversion–output–feedback cycle using a tax-policy example.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Easton’s systems approach and Figure 1.1.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Easton’s “black box” remains a problem
The systems model clarifies interdependence, but it leaves major questions open:

What actually happens inside the conversion process?
Why do political systems process similar demands differently?
Can the model explain democratic collapse or institutional change?
Does naming a system’s components produce a testable explanation?



A framework organizes observation; a theory must also specify causal expectations.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Distinguish a conceptual framework from a causal theory.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), critiques of Easton’s systems approach.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structural functionalism looks beneath labels
Almond and Coleman asked two separate questions:

What structures exist?
What political functions must be performed?


The same function can be performed by different structures:

parties may aggregate interests in one system;
the military, a ruling party, or patronage networks may do so elsewhere;
courts, bureaucracies, or party organs may regulate and adjudicate.


Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Emphasize that similar institutional names do not guarantee similar functions.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), structural-functionalism discussion; Almond and Coleman (1960).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Political systems must perform recurring functions
text:
Political systems must perform recurring functions


Process functions

Interest articulation
Interest aggregation
Policy making
Regulation
Adjudication


System-maintenance functions

Political socialization
Recruitment of leaders
Political communication



Cold call: Which structures perform these functions in China? In Taiwan?

Suggested time: 3 minutes. Accept multiple answers; press students to separate the function from the organization performing it.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Almond’s structural-functional framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structural functionalism also has limits

It assumes system survival is the central goal.
It can portray political systems as static rather than adaptive.
Its categories may reflect Western democratic experience.
It says little about how institutions emerged or changed.



The field escaped narrow formalism, but risked replacing it with abstract concepts that explained too little.


Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. Link the critique back to Macridis: every framework highlights some phenomena and obscures others.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), critique of structural functionalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Post-behavioralism reopened purpose
Critics challenged two behavioralist commitments:

Value-free science: political facts require interpretation, and interpretation cannot be fully separated from values.
Method over substance: technical refinement can displace consequential political questions.


Post-behavioral and constructivist approaches emphasized how political realities and categories are socially constructed.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Avoid presenting this as a rejection of evidence; it is a dispute over objectivity, meaning, and purpose.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), post-behavioral critique; Bay (1965).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Neo-institutionalism brought rules back in
Behavioralism looked beyond formal rules; neo-institutionalism asked what had been lost.


Electoral systems shape representation and party competition.
Executive design shapes coordination and deadlock.
Federal arrangements distribute authority and conflict.
Courts and constitutions structure enforcement and restraint.




Institutions matter because people can redesign rules more readily than they can redesign history, culture, or economic structure.


Suggested time: 2.5 minutes. Stress that institutions interact with context; rules are malleable but never unconstrained.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), neo-institutional movement and constitutional design.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The field comes full circle
Ancient question: What political arrangement supports a good and stable order?
Behavioral correction: Explain politics empirically, beyond formal rules.
Neo-institutional synthesis: Use comparative evidence to understand how rules shape outcomes in context.


Comparative politics becomes applicable again—but with greater methodological discipline.


Suggested time: 1.5 minutes. This resolves the historical arc and returns to the course project.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), conclusion of “The Evolution of Comparative Politics.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Context before design
Ishiyama organizes the book in two stages:


The political “soil”

Historical development
Economy
Political culture and identity
Social structure
International environment


Institutional choices

Electoral system
Executive and legislature
Courts
Federalism and local authority
Interactions among the rules



Design cannot compensate automatically for hostile contextual conditions.

Suggested time: 2 minutes. Explain why the course studies context before institutional options.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), “The Plan of this Book.”

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Your team’s comparative logic
Every team should eventually complete this sentence:

Because our focal country and shadow comparator are similar on [background conditions] but differ on [key factor or outcome], their comparison helps us evaluate the claim that [cause] conditions [outcome].


Then add:

The comparison cannot rule out [rival explanation], so we will seek additional evidence from [source or case].


Suggested time: 3 minutes. Give students 60 seconds to draft a version with one of the course pairings, then hear two examples.
[Sources] - Instructor application of Ishiyama’s comparative-method framework.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Five ideas to carry forward

Comparative politics is a subject and method.
Its central challenge is many explanations, few cases.
MSSD and MDSD create leverage through case selection.
The field repeatedly negotiates values, evidence, and application.
Institutional design works only when evaluated in context.



The standard for this course: make a clear claim, show comparative evidence, and state the limits of the inference.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Use as a retrieval check: hide the body and ask students to name the five ideas first.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Exit question

What makes a comparison persuasive rather than merely interesting?


Submit three sentences:

one claim about a political outcome;
one case pairing that could evaluate it; and
one rival explanation the pairing cannot eliminate.


Suggested time: 2 minutes. Collect in Teams or use as the bridge to the claim–evidence map assignment.
[Sources] - Instructor synthesis based on Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Chapter source
Ishiyama, John T. 2012. Comparative Politics: Principles of Democracy and Democratization. Wiley-Blackwell. Introduction: “Comparative Politics and Democracy.”

This slide provides the student-facing source record for the lecture.
[Sources] - Ishiyama (2012), Introduction.
