title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Why did some states enter the twentieth century with durable democratic institutions while others remained authoritarian or experienced democratic breakdown?


Two readings give us different parts of an answer:

Ishiyama offers a historical explanation across six countries
Lijphart shows how to evaluate comparisons when cases are few and causes are many


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 2. - Lijphart, “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method” (1971), pp. 682–693.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Distinguish a democratic threshold from degrees of polyarchy
Explain Ishiyama’s three historical conditions for democratization
Compare the six country trajectories using common questions
Diagnose the “many variables, small number of cases” problem
Turn a historical narrative into a testable comparative claim

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Opening comparison


Britain

Parliament constrained the Crown before industrialization
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Political inclusion widened gradually


Russia

Autocracy remained dominant
Serfdom and elite dependence persisted
Reform arrived late and was reversed




Cold-call question: Which difference looks most causally important, and what evidence would change your mind?


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, country discussions of Britain and Russia.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: why did wool matter?
Rising Mediterranean demand for English wool changed English politics. Through what mechanism?

Wool revenue let the Crown govern without summoning Parliament
Wool needs much land and little labour, so landlords enclosed the commons
Wool profits paid for the standing army the Stuarts wanted
The wool trade imported Continental ideas about representation



The second. The asymmetry is the whole mechanism: land mattered, labour did not — so the peasantry was displaced and the nobility became commercial.


[Key] The second. This separates students who followed the causal chain from those who retain only “wool was important.”
The first option inverts the political outcome — in England the Crown lost that struggle. The third attaches real Stuart-era material to the wrong mechanism. Both are plausible enough to be worth naming aloud.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: The outcome to explain

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Democracy has more than one definition
text:
Democracy has more than one definition


Schumpeter
Democracy is a method for selecting leaders through a competitive struggle for votes.
This is a narrow, procedural definition.

Held
Democracy requires political equality among members of the political community.
This is a more demanding standard.


The definition determines which cases count as democratic.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of Schumpeter and Held.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Dahl’s polyarchy
Dahl treats democracy as an ideal and uses polyarchy for real political systems.


Competition

Elected officials
Free and fair elections
Freedom of expression
Alternative information
Independent associations


Participation

Broad suffrage
Broad eligibility for office
Equal consideration of preferences



Countries may improve on one dimension without improving equally on the other.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, summary of Dahl (1989).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A democratic threshold
For the study of transitions, Ishiyama uses four minimum components drawn from Linz and Stepan and from Rose, Mishler, and Haerpfer.







Component
Diagnostic question




Rule of law
Are rulers bound by law?


Civil society
Can groups organize independently of the state?


Free and fair elections
Is there meaningful competition for office?


Accountability
Must governing officials answer for their actions?




No single component is sufficient. The combination identifies whether a regime has crossed a democratic threshold.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of the minimal definition of democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two measures answer different questions








Concept
What it measures
Best question




Minimal democracy
A categorical threshold
Has the regime become democratic?


Polyarchy
Degrees of competition and participation
How democratic is the regime?





Democratization first establishes the minimum institutions, then can deepen competition and participation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why does Dahl need a second word?
text:
Check: why does Dahl need a second word?
Dahl reserves democracy for an ideal type and calls real systems polyarchies. Why?

Because existing democracies differ from one another
Because no actual system fully approximates the ideal
Because the term applies only after a completed transition



The second. The ideal is a standard, not a description — so every real case falls short of it, and the question becomes by how much.


[Key] The second option. The common error is the first: students who remember that polyarchies vary along competition and participation mistake a consequence of the term for its reason. The third describes the minimal-threshold approach (Linz and Stepan), not Dahl.
Ask for hands before revealing. If the room splits between one and two, that split is the teaching moment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Ishiyama’s historical argument

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Industrialization as a political shock
Industrialization changes more than production.

New classes seek political influence
Cities and markets unsettle older hierarchies
States face demands for representation and protection
Existing institutions must absorb or repress conflict



Ishiyama treats industrialization as a storm. The outcome depends partly on the political vessel constructed before the storm arrived.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, historical approach and ship metaphor.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Sequence is the central mechanism


Before
National identity, social order, and limits on rulers develop unevenly.

During
Industrialization creates new wealth, classes, conflicts, and demands.

After
Institutions incorporate new groups, break down, or harden into authoritarian rule.


The same economic shock can therefore produce different political outcomes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three historical conditions

Political national identity existed before industrialization
Accountability and rule of law constrained rulers before industrialization
The feudal or old social order had been transformed before industrialization



The argument is configurational. The conditions reinforce each other rather than operating as isolated causes.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, three questions organizing the six cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: which one is not on the list?
text:
Check: which one is not on the list?
Ishiyama organizes all six cases around three conditions established before industrialization. Which of these is not one of them?

A mass national identity
Accountability and the rule of law
The old social order swept away
An industrial working class organized into parties



The fourth. It sounds like something a chapter about industrialization ought to ask — which is exactly why it is worth naming as absent.


[Key] The fourth. Party organization of the working class is not among the three. The point is not trivia: the three conditions are all pre-industrial, and the chapter’s whole argument is that what mattered had already happened before the shock arrived. A condition defined by industrial society could not do that work.
Have them write the three down here. Round 2 asks their team to answer versions of all three about their focal country.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Political national identity
Ishiyama distinguishes cultural community from political unity.







Concept
Basis of membership




Kulturnation
Shared language, culture, religion, or ancestry


Staatsnation
Shared political institutions and a recognized political community





Cultural homogeneity does not automatically produce political integration. Japan was relatively homogeneous, yet its modern political identity had to be constructed.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of cultural and political nationhood.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Accountability before mass politics
The issue is not whether a country already had universal suffrage.
The issue is whether institutions had already established that:

Rulers could be constrained
Revenue and law required bargaining
Organized interests could act outside the state
Political conflict could occur within accepted institutions


Early accountability provided channels through which later demands could enter politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Transformation of the old order
A landed elite may respond to economic change in different ways.


Transformed elite

Wealth becomes commercial
Status depends less on hereditary privilege
Elites can bargain within representative institutions


Persistent old order

Land and labor remain coercively organized
Elites depend on autocratic protection
New groups threaten established privilege



The second path makes democratic inclusion more threatening to incumbent elites.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, use of Barrington Moore and the transformation of feudalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The argument as a causal chain
text:
The argument as a causal chain








Stage
Historical question
Expected consequence




Community
Is there an accepted political nation?
Conflict stays within a shared polity


Constraint
Are rulers accountable under law?
New demands enter established channels


Social order
Has hereditary privilege been transformed?
Elites can tolerate broader participation


Industrial shock
How intense is social disruption?
Earlier arrangements face a stress test


Outcome
Are conflict and inclusion institutionalized?
Democracy, instability, or authoritarianism




[Sources] - Analytical reconstruction from Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Six trajectories

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Britain

Political centralization and national integration developed early
The wool economy and enclosure weakened the traditional peasantry
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Parliament defeated royal absolutism and secured rule-bound bargaining
Suffrage expanded within an already accepted institutional arena



Democratization widened access to the stadium. It did not require constructing a new stadium during the crisis.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Britain section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
France

Absolutism subordinated nobles and weakened independent accountability
Labor-intensive agriculture preserved a large peasantry
The Revolution destroyed noble privilege but did not produce immediate institutional consensus
New social demands repeatedly met resistance outside stable channels
Democratic development lurched through revolution, reaction, and constitutional redesign


France shows partial preparation followed by repeated institutional rupture.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, France section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why did French feudalism survive?
text:
Check: why did French feudalism survive?
England and France faced the same commercial opening. France did not transform. Why not?

The Revolution destroyed the nobility before commercial agriculture could develop
France entered international trade later, delaying commercial pressure
French production was labour-intensive, so landlords kept peasants rather than shedding them
There was no commercial demand for French agricultural products



The third. Viniculture and similar crops needed hands on the land. Same pressure, opposite incentive, opposite outcome.


[Key] The third. The first reverses the sequence — the Revolution came after the failure to transform, and Ishiyama is explicit that it destroyed the nobility while strengthening the peasantry. The fourth is simply false in the chapter: demand rose.
This is the pair’s payoff. Ask why the comparison is informative at all, and the answer is that the crop is the only thing that differs in the relevant respect.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
United States

Colonial assemblies established traditions of representation and accountability
The country lacked European feudalism
A unified political nation remained contested by sectional identity
Slavery sustained hereditary racial privilege in the South
Civil War settled the supremacy of the national state through violence



Institutions arrived early, but national political integration arrived late.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, United States section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Germany

Political fragmentation persisted into the nineteenth century
The Junker elite retained power in Prussia
Unification occurred through authoritarian state-building and war
Industrialization outpaced democratization
Weimar inherited deep cleavages, weak democratic commitment, war debt, and severe crisis


Rapid state formation did not produce an equally rapid democratic settlement.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Germany section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Japan

Tokugawa rule ended civil conflict but preserved decentralized feudal structures
Meiji leaders constructed political identity around loyalty to the emperor
The state directed modernization under external pressure
Old domains and military traditions were adapted rather than fully displaced
Durable democracy followed defeat and postwar institutional reconstruction


Japan separates cultural homogeneity from democratic political integration.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Japan section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Russia

Empire preceded a distinct modern national political community
Loyalty centered on the Tsar and the state
Autocracy destroyed or subordinated alternative centers of power
Serfdom and a dependent nobility persisted
Reform after 1905 left the Tsar’s veto and dissolution powers intact
War and state collapse opened the path to revolution rather than democracy



Russia is Ishiyama’s sharpest contrast with Britain across all three historical conditions.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Russia section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Six cases on common dimensions











Case
Political identity before industrialization
Accountability before industrialization
Transformation of old order
Broad trajectory




Britain
Strong
Strong
Extensive
Gradual inclusion


France
Partial
Weak
Partial
Repeated rupture


United States
Contested
Strong
Mixed because of slavery
Integration through civil war


Germany
Weak
Weak
Uneven
Authoritarian unification, fragile democracy


Japan
Constructed from above
Weak
Partial
State-led modernization, postwar democracy


Russia
Imperial loyalty
Very weak
Minimal
Autocracy, revolution





[Sources] - Synthesis of Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Paired contrast: Britain and France
Both countries experienced commercial change, state formation, and class conflict.







Similar background
Critical difference




Early European states
Parliament constrained the English Crown, while French absolutism prevailed


Powerful landed elites
English elites commercialized more fully, while French landlords retained peasant labor


Industrial and urban pressures
Britain incorporated groups gradually, while France repeatedly rebuilt institutions




This pairing directs attention to accountability and elite transformation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Paired contrast: United States and Germany
text:
Paired contrast: United States and Germany
Both were late projects of national political integration with strong regional divisions.







United States
Germany




Representative institutions preceded full national integration
Authoritarian unification preceded national democratic integration


No European feudal order, but slavery preserved hereditary privilege
Junker privilege persisted within the new state


Civil war consolidated national authority
External war consolidated an authoritarian empire




Similar problems of unity were processed through different institutions.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Paired contrast: Japan and Russia
Both pursued state-led modernization under autocratic authority.

Political identity centered on personal loyalty to the sovereign
Bureaucratic states promoted rapid economic and military change
Older social and military hierarchies persisted
Independent civil society and accountable institutions remained weak



The comparison suggests that modernization alone does not generate democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Lijphart’s design audit

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four ways to study politics








Method
Cases
Control strategy




Experimental
Designed observations
Random assignment or direct manipulation


Statistical
Many
Estimate relationships while controlling for alternatives


Comparative
Few
Select and compare cases to approximate control


Case study
One
Generate, probe, confirm, or challenge theoretical claims





For Lijphart, the comparative method follows the same logic of control as statistical analysis, but with too few cases for conventional statistical control.


[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 682–685.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The central comparative problem

Many plausible explanatory variables, but only a small number of cases.


In Ishiyama’s cases, democratic outcomes may reflect several factors at once.



National identity
Accountability
Agrarian class structure
Timing of industrialization



War and defeat
Religion
State capacity
International intervention




If several causes change together, a comparison cannot easily isolate one effect.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 685–686. - Application to Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four methods, one axis






Figure 1: Lijphart’s four basic methods, arranged by how many cases they work with and how each achieves control. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Lijphart (1971), pp. 682–685.
The figure is clickable — it opens full screen, which is worth doing when you walk the four boxes.
Two things to say aloud. First, the comparative method is one of the basic scientific methods, not the scientific method — Lijphart is explicitly narrower than Lasswell and Almond, who treat comparison and science as the same thing. Second, the orange box at the bottom is the sentence students most often get wrong on assessment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what separates comparative from statistical?
text:
Check: what separates comparative from statistical?
Lijphart says the comparative method resembles the statistical method in every respect but one. Which one?

The comparative method discovers relationships; the statistical method only measures them
Its cases are too few to permit control through partial correlations
It achieves control by deliberate randomization
It is a narrow technique, while the statistical method is a general strategy



The second — and Lijphart goes further. There is no clear dividing line between them: the difference depends entirely on the number of cases.


[Key] The second. The first inverts Lijphart’s own distinction — he insists the comparative method is a method of discovering relationships among variables and is not a method of measurement. The third describes the experimental method; randomization is precisely what nobody can do to countries.
The payoff line: if the only difference is N, then “qualitative versus quantitative” is a difference of degree, not of kind — and the same standards of inference apply to both.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Lijphart’s four responses







Response
Practical move




Increase cases
Add countries, regions, or historical periods


Reduce property space
Combine related categories and variables


Select comparable cases
Hold background conditions as similar as possible


Focus on key variables
Prefer a parsimonious explanation




Each response improves leverage, but each also creates tradeoffs.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 686–690.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
How Ishiyama addresses small N







Lijphart’s response
Ishiyama’s design




Increase cases
Uses six national histories rather than one


Reduce property space
Organizes diverse histories around three conditions


Select comparable cases
Builds paired contrasts with partly shared contexts


Focus on key variables
Emphasizes sequence before industrialization





The chapter gains clarity by simplifying history. That same simplification creates questions about omitted causes and scope.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Comparable means comparable for a question
text:
Comparable means comparable for a question
Cases do not need to be identical.
They need to be similar on factors treated as controls and different on the factor believed to matter.



Stronger pairing
Britain and France for early state development, agrarian change, and constraints on rulers.

Harder pairing
Britain and Japan when geography, external pressure, timing, and institutional inheritance all differ.



Comparability is produced by the research question and the design.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 687–690.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What “comparable” looks like






Figure 2: Comparable cases are alike on everything treated as a control and unlike on the suspected cause and the outcome. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Lijphart (1971), pp. 687–690.
This is the figure to leave on screen while teams talk. It is the logic of their own pairing: the dossier chose two countries precisely so that the green rows hold and the orange rows move.
If a team cannot name what its green rows are, it does not yet have a controlled comparison — it has two countries.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what makes two cases comparable?
text:
Check: what makes two cases comparable?

Similar in as many respects as possible, including the variables you want to relate
Drawn from the same region, since areas supply natural controls
Similar on many characteristics treated as constants, but different on the variables you want to relate
Different in as many respects as possible, so a shared outcome must have a common cause



The third. Cases that are similar in every respect would leave nothing to explain.


[Key] The third. The first is the intuitive error — students hear “comparable” and think “alike in every way.” The second is the area-studies approach, which Lijphart treats as a useful aid but warns can become “a form of imprisonment.” The fourth describes a most-different design.
Say plainly: this is what Round 1 asks each team to defend, and “both are in Africa” is the answer that loses marks.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Case studies can serve different purposes
text:
Case studies can serve different purposes








Type
Role in theory




Atheoretical
Describes a case without engaging a broader proposition


Interpretive
Uses an existing theory to explain a case


Hypothesis-generating
Develops a new proposition from close study


Theory-confirming
Adds a case that fits an existing proposition


Theory-infirming
Adds a case that weakens confidence in a proposition


Deviant
Studies an unexpected case to refine the theory





Hypothesis-generating and deviant cases are especially useful for building better explanations.

[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), pp. 691–693.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Deviant cases refine probabilistic claims
Suppose the claim is:

Early accountability usually increases the chance of durable democratization.


A case with early accountability and democratic failure matters, but it does not automatically disprove the claim.
Questions for the deviant case:

Was accountability genuine or only formal?
Did war or state collapse overwhelm the expected effect?
Does the theory require another condition?
Is the claim limited to a particular historical scope?


[Sources] - Lijphart (1971), discussion of theory-infirming and deviant cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: A design audit of the chapter
text:
A design audit of the chapter


Explanatory gains

Common questions discipline six narratives
Historical sequence identifies plausible mechanisms
Paired contrasts reveal meaningful differences
Cases connect institutions to social structure


Remaining limits

Cases are concentrated in major powers
Several causes move together
Outcome categories are broad
The framework is strongly rooted in Western history



The comparison is valuable when its scope and uncertainty remain explicit.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, concluding caveats. - Lijphart (1971), comparative method limitations.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: After the six cases

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The Third Wave
Huntington coined the phrase in 1991. The wave began in the mid-1970s and gathered speed as the Cold War wound down and the Soviet Union collapsed.

Early optimism assumed that underdevelopment and other structural constraints would not impede democracy’s spread.



Haggard and Kaufman’s summary of what actually happened: the net increase in the number of democracies hid substantial churning, with a steady if small stream of reversions to authoritarian rule.


[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), Annual Review of Political Science 19: 125–144, pp. 126–127.
Connect back to Ishiyama deliberately. Chapter 2 explains six cases that had already democratized by the twentieth century. Haggard and Kaufman survey what happened to everyone else, and they reach a methodological conclusion very close to Lijphart’s.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Transitions to what?
Early work treated the puzzle as the collapse of authoritarian rule — the exit of incumbents, capped by founding elections.

But many Third Wave transitions produced regimes that fell short of democracy on any broader definition:

Competitive authoritarian (Levitsky and Way) · illiberal · electoral authoritarian · hybrid

Elections held, limited political space, but a playing field the incumbent defines.



These are not way stations. A growing recognition is that competitive authoritarianism may be a persistent equilibrium in its own right.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
When two datasets disagree






Figure 3: Cheibub et al. and the Polity Project code the same phenomenon and agree on barely half of it. Click to enlarge.




[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), p. 128.
This is the slide to linger on, because it is the dossier lesson in miniature. Every team’s dossier reports figures that disagree with each other, and every team will be tempted to pick the flattering one.
The honest move is the one Haggard and Kaufman make: say which measure you used, say why, and say what changes if you had used the other.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Structure returned, but without mechanisms
As optimism about “crafting” democracy ebbed, structural theories came back: level of development, inequality, resource endowments, ethnic and religious heterogeneity.

But the findings are mixed almost everywhere you look:







Structural claim
What the evidence does




Inequality drives transitions
Boix finds support; Houle, Ahlquist and Wibbels, and Haggard and Kaufman find no significant relationship


Resource wealth blocks democracy
Contested; Haber and Menaldo find no relationship, and selection bias cuts against the standard test


Ethnic fragmentation destabilizes democracy
Few tests exist; Fish and Brooks, and Fish and Kroenig, find effects disappear with development






Haggard and Kaufman’s diagnosis: the enduring weakness of these theories is inattention to the mechanisms linking structure to regime change.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Development: which question?


Transitions
Does development cause authoritarian regimes to democratize?
Contested. Przeworski et al. argued it does not; Boix and Stokes challenged them using a longer time frame.

Consolidation
Does development help democracies survive?
Much stronger consensus. Przeworski et al.: no democracy had ever reverted above a per capita income of $6,055 — Argentina’s level in 1975.



Same variable, two questions, two very different states of knowledge. Which question you ask decides what the literature can tell you.


[Sources] Haggard and Kaufman (2016), p. 129. Boix shows the result is stronger still in the post–Cold War period.
Worth adding: a number of poor democracies have nonetheless survived a long time — Benin since 1991, Mongolia since 1992, Ghana since 1993, Moldova since 1993. The threshold is a regularity, not a law.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
No taproot

Haggard and Kaufman’s central methodological claim: the quest for an overarching theory of democratization — a taproot — is probably misguided.


Even well-supported cross-national generalizations must accommodate numerous anomalies. Their prescription:

Combinations of causal factors rather than single causes
Alternative pathways to the same outcome
Equifinality — different routes, same destination




Notice what this is not. It is not a call for more data. It is a claim that the assumption of one causal path is the problem.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The same conclusion, from two directions
text:
The same conclusion, from two directions


Lijphart, 1971
Too many variables, too few cases. Control by selecting cases; be modest about what one comparison can establish.

Haggard and Kaufman, 2016
Large-N work yields anomalies. Look for combinations, pathways, equifinality; use qualitative work on necessary and sufficient conditions.



Forty-five years apart, working from opposite ends of the N, and they arrive at the same place: a single general law of democratization is not what this field is going to produce.


This is the slide that justifies the course design. The team project asks for a diagnosis of one country against one comparator — not a theory of democratization. Haggard and Kaufman are the reason that is the right ambition rather than a modest one.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: what follows from “no taproot”?
Haggard and Kaufman argue the search for an overarching theory is misguided. What do they conclude the field should do?

Build larger cross-national datasets, since samples are too small to detect the true effect
Attend to combinations of causal factors, alternative pathways, and equifinality
Move to formal models that specify precise conditions
Agree on one measure of democracy, since disagreement is mostly definitional



The second. More data would not help if the problem is the assumption of a single path.


[Key] The second. The first is the instinct almost everyone has — anomalies mean underpowered tests — and it is exactly what they argue against.
The fourth is tempting after the measurement slide. Note the difference: they do think measurement matters a great deal, but they never suggest one agreed measure would dissolve the theoretical problem.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: development and democracy
On development, where is the consensus in the literature stronger?

Transitions — development reliably causes authoritarian regimes to democratize
Consolidation — development is associated with democracies surviving
Neither, since the correlation disappears once region is controlled
Resource wealth specifically, now agreed to be the decisive form of development



The second. The transition question remains contested; the survival question is where the evidence is strongest.


[Key] The second. The first states the classic modernization claim, which Haggard and Kaufman report as contested — Przeworski et al. against Boix and Stokes.
If students remember only one thing from this pair of slides, it should be that “does development cause democracy?” is two questions wearing one coat.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 6: From reading to research

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A claim-evidence map








Element
Example




Claim
Early constraints on rulers make later democratic inclusion more durable.


Mechanism
New groups can pursue demands through accepted institutions rather than extra-institutional conflict.


Evidence for
Britain had parliamentary constraint before industrialization and expanded participation gradually.


Comparative evidence
France developed under absolutism and repeatedly experienced rupture during inclusion.


Rival explanation
Different agrarian class structures, not accountability, drove the contrast.


Discriminating evidence
Compare cases with similar agrarian structures but different levels of early accountability.


Scope
European states undergoing early industrialization.





[Sources] - Example synthesized from Ishiyama, Chapter 2, using Lijphart’s logic of control.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Team comparison workshop
For the focal country and shadow comparator:

Record each country’s value on Ishiyama’s three historical conditions
Identify one outcome that differs between the countries
State one causal claim that could explain the difference
Name one rival explanation
Identify evidence that would distinguish the two explanations



The goal is not to find two identical countries. The goal is to make the basis of comparison explicit.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A stronger team presentation
An effective weekly presentation includes:

One comparative puzzle
One explicit causal claim
Evidence from both countries
One rival explanation
One limitation of the comparison
One question for the class


The presenters defend the comparison. The class serves as the design review panel.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
History constrains without determining
Ishiyama rejects a mechanical reading of the argument.

Long-term structures shape the options available to leaders
Critical moments still involve political choices
Institutions can redirect inherited conflict
External shocks can alter trajectories



Historical conditions change probabilities. They do not write an unavoidable political future.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, conclusion and discussion of critical choices.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: constraint or destiny?
Ishiyama cites Sartori to warn against one reading of the six cases. Which?

Historical factors describe background conditions but explain nothing
Democracy was the product of human choices at critical moments, though choices were constrained
Every case is unique, so comparison cannot support generalization
Institutions matter only after a country has crossed the democratic threshold



The second. Democracy “did not just happen, nor was it predetermined by history or culture” — but leaders cannot engineer it where no social or economic base supports it.


[Key] The second. The first overstates: Ishiyama says historical factors are useful for describing background conditions, just not determinative. The third is the opposite of the chapter’s purpose.
This is the one to spend a minute on. If history determined outcomes there would be nothing for a constitutional engineer to do, and the team paper would be incoherent. A student who misses this has not yet understood what they are writing in December.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Core takeaways

Definitions determine the outcome we are trying to explain
Ishiyama emphasizes the sequence of identity, accountability, and social transformation before industrialization
The six histories become comparable only when organized by common questions
Lijphart identifies the central weakness of the design: many causes and few cases
Pairing, parsimony, rival explanations, and deviant cases can strengthen comparative inference
